content: 1. Scaling up the provision of lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV requires a thorough review of the infrastructure and operational implications. Countries may adopt a phased approach, starting with an early learning phase before full-scale implementation. 2. It is essential to establish clear linkages to care and patient transfer systems. Decisions must be made regarding whether women will continue receiving ART at the site providing antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) or if they will be transferred to an existing ART site. Strategies must be implemented to minimize the risk of women being lost to care during these transitions. 3. Human resource requirements must be carefully reviewed. Many staff at PMTCT sites have limited training and experience in providing ART, particularly in settings where Option A has been implemented for PMTCT. Capacity-building, task shifting, and potential expansion of health personnel may be necessary to enable PMTCT sites to manage the additional responsibility of providing lifelong ART. 4. Promoting adherence to therapy and retention in care is particularly challenging during the postpartum breastfeeding period. Strategies must be developed to monitor and support adherence and retention, as well as to re-engage women and their HIV-exposed children who are lost to follow-up. 5. Ethical issues must be considered. Initiating lifelong ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women, regardless of CD4 count, may create temporary disparities in treatment access. For example, a pregnant woman with a high CD4 count may continue ART after delivery, while her husband or other family members with lower CD4 counts may not yet be eligible for treatment. Policies and strategies must address these disparities and leverage the enrollment of women into lifelong treatment to promote a family-centered approach, including HIV testing and treatment for partners and household members. 6. Ensuring the quality of HIV testing is critical. Quality-assurance programs, including for rapid HIV testing, must be developed to ensure accurate and reliable results. Proper use of testing algorithms is essential for optimal implementation across all areas of the country. 7. Laboratory monitoring needs must be assessed. While CD4 testing may not be required to initiate ART in pregnant women, monitoring for toxicity and ART response, including viral load testing, should be available to assess viral suppression. Infant diagnosis is also crucial to identify HIV-infected infants and link them to appropriate treatment and care. Surveillance systems should be established to evaluate the impact of ART on birth defects, pregnancy outcomes, and safety among infants and young children exposed through breastfeeding. 8. Adequate monitoring and evaluation frameworks must be implemented. High-quality, longitudinal cohort data on mothers and their HIV-exposed infants across various service delivery points and the continuum of care are necessary. The true effectiveness of PMTCT programs depends on infant infection status and HIV-free survival at the end of the breastfeeding period, not just early infection status at six weeks of age. 9. Infant prophylaxis is particularly critical in cases of late maternal HIV diagnosis, limited or no antepartum ART, or interruptions in maternal ART due to toxicity, intolerance, or non-adherence. 10. A continuous and uninterrupted drug supply is essential for maternal ART during pregnancy and breastfeeding to ensure PMTCT and maternal health. Adequate drug forecasting and supply chain management are critical to prevent stock-outs and treatment interruptions. 11. Lifelong ART (Option B+) for all pregnant and breastfeeding women is particularly relevant in settings with generalized epidemics, high repeat pregnancy rates, low family planning coverage, low partner testing rates, limited access to CD4 testing, low ART coverage for eligible pregnant women, and prolonged breastfeeding durations. 12. Providing ART only during the period of risk for mother-to-child transmission (Option B) and continuing lifelong ART only for women meeting standard eligibility criteria is more relevant in settings with concentrated epidemics, lower repeat pregnancy rates, higher family planning coverage, high access to CD4 testing, high ART coverage for eligible pregnant women, and safe formula feeding options. 13. In high-fertility settings, family planning programs should be prioritized to help women avoid unplanned pregnancies. 14. Programs should determine which clinical and laboratory services will be available at each level of the healthcare delivery system. The optimal model for ART decentralization depends on the local context. 15. Human resource policies and task shifting should be considered. All health workers, including community health workers, must be regularly trained, mentored, and supervised to ensure high-quality care and implementation of updated national recommendations. Task shifting may be necessary to ensure an appropriate mix of health workers at peripheral facilities. 16. Strategies for retaining staff in rural or remote areas must be developed and implemented to address high turnover and attrition rates. 17. Strengthening linkages and referral systems is essential. Community-based treatment programs must be linked with regular care at health facilities and supported by adequate laboratory, diagnostic, monitoring, evaluation, and drug supply management systems. 18. An efficient division of responsibilities among national, provincial, regional, and district levels of the health system is crucial to minimize duplication and optimize resource use. Roles should align with capacity, and lines of authority and accountability must be clear and well understood. 19. Partnerships with national regulatory bodies, professional associations, and other stakeholders are necessary to address the scope of practice, roles, and responsibilities of health workers. 20. Expanding ART coverage should be the first priority, as all treatment regimens reduce morbidity and mortality. Early diagnosis and prompt ART initiation are especially critical for infants and young children, who are at greater risk of poor outcomes. 21. Strengthening links between diagnosis and treatment is essential to minimize losses to follow-up and improve ART uptake among children. Family-based approaches to HIV testing and provider-initiated testing and counseling are important strategies to increase diagnosis and treatment among children. 22. Accelerating regulatory approval of preferred ARV formulations, such as scored dispersible fixed-dose combinations for children, is critical to support ART scale-up in remote areas. 23. Countries should phase out the use of d4T in favor of safer alternatives like TDF, which is more effective and has fewer side effects. A costed phase-out plan should be developed, including investments in laboratory strengthening and capacity-building. 24. Adequate forecasting and procurement of preferred alternative drugs are essential to avoid stock-outs and treatment interruptions during the transition away from d4T. 25. Training and education for clinic staff and ART patients are necessary to ensure a smooth transition to new regimens. 26. Leveraging existing infrastructure and channels to make ART available for children wherever adult ART and PMTCT interventions are provided is key to improving access and uptake. 27. Family-based care strategies should be designed and implemented to support retention and adherence among children, taking into account the unique challenges faced by children who move between households.
